parsed.thesis: Authority does not transfer through copying: a snapshot, cache, or transcription is only a claim about the source at a past moment, not the fact itself. Derived state is safe to use only when it carries verifiable provenance (a source fingerprint) and is re-checked against the authoritative source at every propagation point (merge/sync) and every consumption point (user-facing output); on divergence, the source wins and the mismatch must be surfaced. Staleness must be detectable by design rather than prevented by vigilance, and every correction must harden into an automatic gate so the same class of error cannot recur.

principleCandidate.rationale: The root cause of the failure chain was not one bad read but the absence of any mechanism distinguishing 'transcribed snapshot' from 'source of truth': the 12:00 merge trusted a stale snapshot, the 19:08 broadcast consumed the already-merged staleness, and the first correction was never codified, so the error repeated. Requiring every derived snapshot to carry a verifiable fingerprint (mtime + content hash of its source) and enforcing freshness gates at both propagation and consumption makes staleness cheap to detect by design, aligns all sessions on a single authoritative source, and converts corrections into durable guardrails instead of one-time fixes.
principleCandidate.scope: Applies whenever state is copied, cached, transcribed, synchronized, or merged across sessions, components, or time, and whenever derived representations feed decisions or user-facing output — especially cross-session continuity, heartbeat/scheduled sync jobs, and announcements built on cached records. Less critical for ephemeral reads of a live source that are never propagated.

risks: Adjacent to existing axioms: this principle extends T-03 (evidence before inference), T-07 (verify after acting), and T-10 (persist key state); it does not contradict them, but the axiom set should avoid accumulating redundant overlapping guidance.
Verification overhead: mandatory fingerprint checks at every merge and consumption point add latency and cost; for low-stakes, high-frequency reads the gate may need proportionality or batching.
Fingerprint equality is not semantic correctness: a snapshot may match the source's mtime+hash yet encode a faulty transformation; freshness gates detect staleness, not derivation bugs.

Misidentified source of truth: if the designated authoritative source is wrong (e.g., pointing at a deprecated file), all freshness gates will systematically validate against a non-authoritative source.
Abort-on-mismatch behavior: automatically blocking user-facing actions on divergence can reduce availability; a human-confirmation fallback may be preferable to a hard stop.
Model-level redesign (attaching fingerprints to every snapshot) carries migration cost and may be over-engineering for small, single-session systems.

principleDraft.title: Derived state is a claim, not a fact: re-verify source provenance at merge and use
principleDraft.statement: Whenever state is copied, cached, transcribed, or synchronized, treat the derived copy as a claim about its source at a past moment, never as the fact itself: (1) attach verifiable provenance to the derived copy — the identity of the authoritative source plus a content fingerprint (e.g., content hash and/or modification timestamp) captured at copy time; (2) before propagating the copy (merge/sync) and before consuming it for decisions or user-facing output, re-read the source's current fingerprint and compare it against the copy's recorded provenance; (3) on divergence, resolve in favor of the authoritative source, refresh the derived copy, and explicitly surface the mismatch; (4) after any staleness correction, codify the freshness check as an automatic gate at that propagation or consumption point so the same class of error cannot silently recur. Ephemeral reads of a live source that are never propagated or persisted are exempt.
principleDraft.rationale: The diagnosed failure chain — a 12:00 merge that trusted a stale snapshot, a 19:08 broadcast that consumed the already-merged staleness, and a correction that was never codified so the error repeated — shows the root cause was not one bad read but the absence of any mechanism distinguishing a transcribed snapshot from the source of truth. Making staleness mechanically detectable by design (fingerprint comparison at defined checkpoints) closes every link in that chain: propagation gates stop stale copies from being merged, consumption gates stop them from reaching users, source-wins resolution realigns state on divergence, and gate codification converts one-time fixes into durable prevention instead of relying on operator vigilance.
applicability: Cross-session continuity: loading persisted memory/session state into a new session and merging it with current state
Scheduled or heartbeat-driven sync/merge jobs that copy authoritative records into shared or derived stores
User-facing output and decisions built on cached, transcribed, or summarized representations of an authoritative source
Pipelines where a snapshot is transcribed, transformed, or summarized before downstream use
Scope boundary: ephemeral reads of a live source that are never propagated or persisted are out of scope
antiPatterns: Merging or syncing a snapshot/cache into shared state without comparing its recorded source fingerprint against the current authoritative source
Broadcasting or acting on derived records (announcements, reports, decisions) without re-checking them against their source at the point of consumption
Propagating derived state that carries no provenance (no source identity or content fingerprint), leaving staleness undetectable
On divergence, silently keeping or propagating the derived copy instead of the authoritative source without surfacing the mismatch
Fixing a staleness incident as a one-time manual correction without codifying an automatic freshness gate, allowing the same error class to recur
Relying on vigilance ('remember to check freshness') instead of a mechanical, by-design staleness check

intentContract.ownerIntent: Prevent the agent from merging or broadcasting stale copies of authoritative records as if they were current — e.g., announcing user-facing status from a cached snapshot without re-verifying it against the live source.
intentContract.targetBehavior: In any tool trajectory involving cached or transcribed state, a reviewer can see the agent record or read a source fingerprint (source identity plus hash/timestamp) alongside the derived copy, re-compare it against the authoritative source immediately before each merge/sync and before each user-facing use, refresh from the source and report the mismatch on divergence, and add a recurring automatic check (not a one-time manual fix) after correcting a staleness incident.
intentContract.forbiddenBehavior: Consuming or propagating derived state (snapshots, caches, transcriptions) as authoritative without any freshness verification at the propagation or consumption point, and leaving staleness corrections as uncodified manual fixes so the same stale-data error repeats.
intentContract.evidenceSource: The diagnosed failure chain: the 12:00 merge trusted a stale snapshot as authoritative, the 19:08 broadcast consumed the already-merged staleness into user-facing output, and the first correction was never codified, so the error repeated.
intentContract.validationExpectation: An evaluator should accept a rule only if it mandates a mechanical fingerprint comparison (source identity plus content hash/timestamp) at both merge/sync and user-facing consumption points, source-wins resolution with the mismatch surfaced, and codification of corrections as automatic gates; rules that merely urge 'keep data current' or 'double-check caches' without an observable check are not faithful.

risks: Overlaps with core axioms T-03 (use observable evidence before claiming results) and T-07 (verify after acting), and is adjacent to T-10 (persist important state): rule generation must scope rules to the derived-state/staleness specialization so they extend rather than duplicate or weaken those axioms.

Mandatory fingerprint checks at every merge and consumption point add latency and cost; applied without proportionality this over-burdens low-stakes, high-frequency reads (batching or proportional gating may be needed).
A matching fingerprint proves freshness, not derivation correctness — a faithfully copied but semantically faulty transformation still passes the gate.
If the designated authoritative source is itself wrong or deprecated, all freshness gates will systematically validate against a non-authoritative source.
Hard abort-on-mismatch before user-facing actions can reduce availability; a surfaced-mismatch-plus-confirmation fallback may be preferable to a silent hard stop.
Requiring provenance metadata on every snapshot is a model-level redesign with migration cost and may over-engineer small, single-session systems.

principleDraft.statement: Whenever state is copied, cached, transcribed, or synchronized across sessions or time, and whenever derived state feeds user-facing output, treat the snapshot as a claim about the source, never as the fact itself. Every derived snapshot must carry verifiable provenance: a fingerprint of its authoritative source (mtime + content hash). At every propagation point (merge/sync/heartbeat) and every consumption point (broadcast/announcement/publish), re-verify the snapshot's fingerprint against the live authoritative source; on divergence the source wins: re-sync from the source, surface the mismatch, and do not propagate or publish the stale state. Every staleness correction must be codified into an automatic verification gate so the same class of error cannot recur.
principleDraft.rationale: The root cause was not one bad read but the absence of any mechanism distinguishing 'transcribed snapshot' from 'source of truth': the 12:00 heartbeat merge trusted the stale snapshot (the deprecated 09-05 version) without checking source mtime/content, the 19:08 broadcast then consumed the already-merged staleness, and the first correction was never codified, so the error recurred and forced a second user correction. Fingerprint provenance plus mandatory freshness gates at both propagation and consumption points makes staleness cheaply detectable by design rather than prevented by vigilance, aligns all sessions on a single authoritative source, and converts one-time fixes into durable guardrails.

parsed.thesis: Stale state propagates when transcribed or cached representations (session snapshots, summaries, replicas) are treated as facts rather than as provisional caches. Trust must be anchored in a single authoritative source: state changes are persisted durably outside volatile sessions, and any consequential use—merging across sessions or emitting to users—must pass an explicit consistency check against that source, with past user corrections compiled into gates that block recurrence.

principleDraft.rationale: The diagnosed failure was systemic, not incidental: the synchronization design treated session snapshots as equivalent fact sources, so stale references survived the merge and re-emerged in user-facing output, forcing the user to correct the same staleness repeatedly. Designating a single authoritative source, verifying cached representations against it at the moment of consequential use (pre-merge, pre-emit), persisting state changes outside volatile sessions, and turning the first correction into a blocking rule stops stale state at the boundary instead of after user-visible errors.
applicability: Cross-session state merges and synchronization designs where session snapshots, replicas, or summaries coexist with a primary source
User-facing output derived from cached, mirrored, or transcribed state (responses, documentation, generated artifacts)
Any read of a cached representation at a consequential boundary (merge, sync, emit) where an authoritative source is distinguishable
Recurring corrections of the same stale reference, where a prior user correction should become a standing gate
Not applicable when no authoritative source exists or when verification cost demonstrably exceeds the downside of staleness
antiPatterns: Treating session snapshots, summaries, or replicas as equivalent fact sources during merges without checking them against the authoritative source
Emitting user-facing content from cached state without a pre-emit consistency check (hash, version, or mtime) against the authoritative source
Persisting critical state changes only inside volatile session context that disappears on session close
Re-accepting a representation the user has already corrected once, without a blocking gate that prevents the same stale reference from recurring
Applying unbounded verification on every read instead of confining checks to consequential boundaries

intentContract.ownerIntent: The Owner wants the agent to stop letting stale, previously-corrected references propagate into merged state and user-facing output by treating session snapshots and other caches as authoritative facts.
intentContract.targetBehavior: Before any merge, synchronization, or user-facing emit that consumes cached or transcribed state, the agent performs an explicit consistency check against the designated authoritative source (content hash, version, or mtime), blocks the action on mismatch, persists state changes durably outside the volatile session, and installs a blocking gate after the first user correction of a stale reference.
intentContract.forbiddenBehavior: Merging or emitting state derived from session snapshots, replicas, or summaries without verifying them against the authoritative source, thereby letting stale or already-corrected references survive the merge and re-emerge in user-visible output that the user must correct again.
intentContract.evidenceSource: The diagnosed pain: a state synchronization design that defaulted to treating session snapshots as equivalent fact sources, so stale references survived a cross-session merge, re-emerged in user-facing output, and forced repeated user correction of the same stale state.
intentContract.validationExpectation: An evaluator should require that any rule derived from this principle mandates a pre-merge/pre-emit consistency check against the authoritative source at consequential boundaries, durable persistence of state changes outside volatile sessions, and conversion of first-time corrections into blocking gates; a rule that permits acting on unverified cached state at those boundaries contradicts this intent and must be flagged rather than accepted.

risks: Partial overlap with core axioms T-03 (use observable evidence before claiming results) and T-07 (verify outcome after acting): this principle specializes them into pre-use cache verification at action boundaries, and downstream rule generation must avoid emitting a generic duplicate of those axioms
Unbounded verification on every read could add latency and load; checks must be confined to consequential boundaries such as merge and emit, or the principle may be over-applied

If the designated authoritative source is wrong or multiple legitimate writers exist, rigid single-source authority may discard valid divergent updates; conflict-resolution rules must be defined alongside the authority designation
Persisted deprecation and version markers add write overhead and can themselves go stale, potentially blocking valid reads if markers are not maintained
Ambiguity in what counts as a 'consequential boundary' could cause inconsistent enforcement; the boundary set (merge, sync, user-facing emit) must be made explicit in derived rules

parsed.thesis: A snapshot of state is testimony, not truth. Any derived representation—session snapshot, cache, summary—is only a hypothesis about its authoritative source, and its authority must be re-established by verifiable fingerprints (mtime, content hash) at every consequential boundary. Because remembering having read something is not evidence of it being current, staleness must be detectable via persisted version fingerprints and structurally forbidden from entering downstream transitions, with user corrections treated as feedback that invalidates and refreshes all affected derived state.

principleCandidate.title: Revalidate derived state against source fingerprints before consequential use
principleCandidate.rationale: The root cause is not one bad merge but the absence of staleness detection: volatile snapshots lacked version fingerprints anchored to the source of truth, so downstream consumers could not distinguish fresh from stale and stale state propagated to the user twice. Requiring fingerprint revalidation (mtime + content hash) at each consumption boundary—merge, broadcast, decision—and encoding fingerprint mismatch as a forbidden input makes staleness structurally impossible to consume, rather than relying on in-session vigilance. Persisting the fingerprint outside volatile context also gives corrections a concrete target to invalidate and refresh.
principleCandidate.scope: Applies whenever state derived from an authoritative source (files, databases, external systems) crosses a boundary—session, process, or time—and is then used for consequential actions such as merging, broadcasting, or deciding. Especially relevant to long-running or multi-session workflows where volatile context can outlive the freshness of what it cached.

risks: Partial overlap with existing core axioms: this principle is a composite of T-03 (observable evidence), T-05 (guardrail encoding), T-07 (verify after action), and T-10 (durable state); if promoted, it should be framed as the derived-state-specific synthesis of these, not a duplicate axiom.
Fingerprint revalidation on every consumption boundary adds latency and I/O cost; over-applying it in low-stakes, high-frequency paths may degrade performance without proportional benefit.

Unstable source metadata (e.g., mtime updates without content change) can cause false staleness, triggering unnecessary refreshes or blocked outputs; fingerprints should rely on content hashes to mitigate.
Blocking downstream actions on mismatch needs a defined fallback path (refresh-then-proceed, or degrade with alert); otherwise time-sensitive outputs like heartbeats may silently stall.
Assuming the source file is always authoritative can be wrong when newer user intent lives in the session; rigidly deferring to the source could overwrite legitimate fresher edits.

principleDraft.title: Revalidate derived state against source fingerprints before consequential use
principleDraft.statement: Whenever state derived from an authoritative source (session snapshot, cache, summary) is about to cross a consequential boundary—merge, broadcast to the user, or state-mutating decision—the agent must revalidate it against a persisted version fingerprint (content hash, with mtime only as a fast-path hint) of that source: proceed only on fingerprint match; on mismatch or missing fingerprint, refresh from the source or halt via a defined fallback before acting. Fingerprints must be persisted outside volatile session context, and user corrections must be treated as invalidation events that mark all affected derived state for refresh.
principleDraft.rationale: The root cause was not a single bad merge but the absence of staleness detection: volatile snapshots carried no version fingerprints anchored to the source of truth, so downstream consumers could not distinguish fresh from stale, stale state propagated to the user twice, and corrections had nothing concrete to invalidate. Fingerprint revalidation at each consumption boundary encodes mismatch as a forbidden input, making staleness structurally impossible to consume rather than dependent on in-session vigilance; persisting the fingerprint outside volatile context provides the durable invalidation target that corrections require.
applicability: State derived from an authoritative source (files, databases, external systems) that crosses a session, process, or time boundary before later use
Long-running or multi-session workflows where in-context caches or summaries can outlive the freshness of what they captured
Consequential boundaries specifically: merging session-derived data with source-of-truth data, broadcasting outputs to the user, and making state-mutating decisions
Handling user corrections that contradict previously captured derived state
antiPatterns: Trusting an in-session cache, snapshot, or summary as current simply because it was read earlier in the session
Merging or broadcasting derived state without comparing the source's current fingerprint against the fingerprint persisted at capture time
Keeping freshness or version information only in volatile context that is lost when the session ends
Letting stale-derived state pass downstream with a warning instead of a hard stop or forced refresh
Relying on mtime alone as the staleness signal where content hashes are available
Ignoring a user correction that contradicts cached derived state instead of invalidating and refreshing it

intentContract.targetBehavior: In the tool trajectory, the agent computes and compares the source's current fingerprint (content hash, mtime as hint) against the fingerprint persisted at capture time before every merge, broadcast, or state-mutating decision, and on mismatch visibly refreshes from the source or halts via a defined fallback instead of using the stale copy.
intentContract.forbiddenBehavior: Consuming or propagating derived state across a consequential boundary without revalidating it against the source's current fingerprint, allowing stale snapshots to silently reach merges, user-facing broadcasts, or decisions.
intentContract.evidenceSource: The diagnosed pain: a stale session snapshot was merged with source-of-truth data and stale state was broadcast to the user a second time, because volatile snapshots carried no version fingerprints anchored to the source of truth, making staleness undetectable and leaving corrections without an invalidation target.
intentContract.validationExpectation: An evaluator should accept a rule only if it demands an observable fingerprint comparison against a persisted record at each consequential boundary, hard-stops or refreshes on mismatch via a defined fallback, and treats user corrections as invalidation events; a change that permits warning-only propagation of stale state or drops the persisted-fingerprint requirement contradicts this intent.

Revalidating fingerprints at every consumption boundary adds latency and I/O cost; over-applying it in low-stakes, high-frequency paths may degrade performance without proportional benefit.

principleDraft.title: Revalidate derived state against source-file fingerprints before consequential use
principleDraft.statement: State derived from an authoritative source (session snapshot, cache, summary) must never enter a consequential transition — merge, sync, heartbeat, broadcast, user-facing decision — without first re-establishing its currency against that source via persisted version fingerprints (content hash as the primary signal, mtime as supporting signal). On mismatch or missing fingerprints the derived state is stale: it must be refreshed from the source, or the action blocked with an alert, never consumed as-is. A user correction that exposes staleness must invalidate and refresh every derived artifact anchored to the affected source so the same stale reference cannot recur.
principleDraft.rationale: The diagnosed root cause is not one bad merge but the absence of staleness detection: cross-session sync treated session-record snapshots as the default source of truth, so a deprecated 09-05 08:24 snapshot flowed unchecked into the 12:00 heartbeat merge and the 19:08 broadcast, forcing the user to correct the same error twice. Anchoring snapshots to verifiable source fingerprints and rechecking them at each consumption boundary turns freshness into observable evidence rather than an assumption, encodes fingerprint mismatch as a forbidden input (a structural guardrail instead of in-session vigilance), and gives user corrections a concrete target to invalidate, closing the repeat-error loop.
applicability: Cross-session or cross-process state synchronization where a snapshot of source state (file, database, external system) crosses a session or time boundary and is later consumed.
Consequential consumption boundaries: heartbeat merges, syncs, broadcasts/announcements, and decisions whose output reaches the user.
Long-running or multi-session workflows where volatile session context can outlive the freshness of what it cached.
Pipelines where derived representations (caches, transcripts, summaries) stand in for an authoritative source of truth.
antiPatterns: Treating a session record, transcript, or cached snapshot as the source of truth by default and consuming it without comparing it to the authoritative source.
Executing a heartbeat merge or broadcast on a snapshot whose mtime/content hash was never checked against the source file.
Declaring a merge/sync successful without comparing the propagated payload against the actual source content.
Re-consuming an affected snapshot after a user correction without invalidating and re-deriving it from the corrected source.
Storing version fingerprints only in volatile in-session memory where a later session cannot use them to detect staleness.

intentContract.targetBehavior: Before each merge/sync/broadcast, the agent reads the authoritative source's fingerprints (content hash, mtime), compares them to the fingerprints captured with the snapshot being consumed, and on mismatch refreshes from the source and alerts rather than proceeding; after a user correction, it invalidates and re-derives all snapshots anchored to the affected source.
intentContract.forbiddenBehavior: Consuming a derived snapshot (session record, cache, summary) as fact in a merge or broadcast without verifying it against the source file's mtime/content hash, propagating deprecated state and repeating the same stale-reference error after a user correction.
